## December 21, 2017

For our final 2017 update, we present:

1.   **Five New Planets:** The following planets have been added, bringing our total number of confirmed planets to **3,572**: [HD 176986](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=hd+176986&type=PLANET_HOST): [b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=hd+176986+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET)&[c](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=hd+176986+c&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET); [K2-18](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=K2-18&type=PLANET_HOST): [c](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=k2-18+c&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET); [GJ 3942](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=GJ+3942&type=PLANET_HOST): [b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=GJ+3942+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET); and [PSR J2322-2650](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=PSR+J2322-2650&type=PLANET_HOST): [b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=PSR+J2322-2650+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET). 
**_Fun Fact:_**PSR J2322-2650 b is only the _sixth_ planet known to orbit a pulsar star, and the first to be discovered since 2011. In fact, there are currently only four pulsar stars known to host exoplanets. See the [Confirmed Planets interactive table](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/TblView/nph-tblView?app=ExoTbls&config=planets) to find out which ones (and for the data on this week's new planets)!

Also, check out our updated video of [planet discoveries by method since 1989](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/videos/mass_period_movie_nexsci.mp4).

2.   **K2 Light Curves from Five Campaigns:** We've added light curves from campaigns 1, 10, 11, 12, and 13 to the archive. Access them through the [K2 Targets Search](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/TblSearch/nph-tblSearchInit?app=ExoTbls&config=k2targets) interface (specify a campaign number, click **Submit Search**, then click on **Download Data Products** and select **Download Results Time Series Wget Script**). 
![Image 2](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/images/news/k2-lightcurve-dl.png)

3.   **K2 Candidates Table Update:** The [K2 Candidates table](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/TblView/nph-tblView?app=ExoTbls&config=k2candidates) is up-to-date after the completion of some necessary updates to the database. The table now includes all K2 candidates named in the published literature, including those in [Petigura et al. (2017)](http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018AJ....155...21P) and [Dressing et al. (2017)](http://adsabs.harvard.edu/cgi-bin/bib_query?arXiv:1703.07416), which brings the total number of unique K2 planet candidates (or confirmed) to **622**.
4.   **See you in January!** The NASA Exoplanet Archive staff will be on break Dec. 23 through Jan. 1, during which there will be no data or software updates. Responses to Helpdesk tickets and social media may also be delayed. If you are attending the American Astronomical Society (AAS) winter meeting in Washington, D.C., stop by the NExScI booth and say hello!

## December 14, 2017

**System With Most Exoplanets Added to the Archive!**

An eighth planet has been found around [KOI-351](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=koi-351&type=PLANET_HOST), also known as Kepler-90, making it the only known system with the same number of planets as our own Solar system. The new planet, KOI-351 i (or, Kepler-90 i, as it's named in the media), has been added to the archive this week and you can view its [Confirmed Planet Overview page](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=KOI-351+i&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET), read the discovery paper by [Shallue et al. (2017)](https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/~avanderb/kepler90i.pdf), and read the [NASA press release](https://www.nasa.gov/press-release/artificial-intelligence-nasa-data-used-to-discover-eighth-planet-circling-distant-star).

We've also added two additional new planets: [Kepler-80](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=kepler-80&type=PLANET_HOST)[g](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=kepler-80+g&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET) and [K2-139](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=K2-139&type=PLANET_HOST)[b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=k2-139+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET). Parameters for all three new planets can be found on their respective Confirmed Planets Overview pages, as well as the [Confirmed Planet interactive table](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/TblView/nph-tblView?app=ExoTbls&config=planets).

**Note:** The eighth planet and its host star are listed as **KOI-351 i** and **KOI-351**, respectively, in the [Confirmed Planets interactive table](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/TblView/nph-tblView?app=ExoTbls&config=planets). When using our Explore the Archive search interface on the home page, you may enter either the KOI or Kepler name and get the same result.

![Image 3: KOI-351 planets as viewed in Confirmed Planets interactive table](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/images/news/confirmed-planets-tbl-koi-351.jpg)

## December 11, 2017

New this week:

*   **UKIRT Microlensing Survey Data**: We've added almost 18 million light curves from the 2015 and 2016 UKIRT microlensing campaigns. See the [UKIRT Bulk Download](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/docs/UKIRTBulkDownload.html) page to get all 75 GB, or search for a subset and browse them in an interactive table by way of our [UKIRT search interface](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/TblSearch/nph-tblSearchInit?app=ExoTbls&config=ukirttimeseries). Read the [documentation](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/docs/UKIRTMission.html) for more information. 
Many thanks to the UKIRT science team for providing these data to our user community.

*   **Now Serving: K2 Campaign 16 Targets**: The K2 mission's Campaign 16 target list is now available through the [K2 Targets Search](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/TblSearch/nph-tblSearchInit?app=ExoTbls&config=k2targets) interface. To see the list, enter **16** as a K2 Campaign column constraint and click **Submit Search**. 
![Image 4](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/images/news/k2c16targets.png)
[](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/docs/2017news.html)
## December 1, 2017

Six new planets were added this week:

*   [HD 76920](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=hd+76920&type=PLANET_HOST)[b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=hd+76920+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET): The most eccentric planet orbiting an evolved star.
*   [HD 40956](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=hd+40956&type=PLANET_HOST)[b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=hd+40956+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET), [HD 111591](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=hd+111591&type=PLANET_HOST)[b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=hd+111591+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET), and [HD 113996](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=hd+113996&type=PLANET_HOST)[b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=hd+113996+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET): Three long-period super-Jupiters orbiting K giants.
*   [OGLE-2016-BLG-1190L](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=OGLE+2016-BLG-1190L&type=PLANET_HOST)[b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=OGLE+2016-BLG-1190L+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET): A planet that falls right on the boundary between planet and brown dwarf.
*   [OGLE-2016-BLG-0613L AB](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=OGLE+2016-BLG-0613L+AB&type=PLANET_HOST)[b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=OGLE+2016-BLG-0613L+AB+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET): A microlensing planet in a binary system.

See the [Confirmed Planets](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/TblView/nph-tblView?app=ExoTbls&config=planets) table for the new data, or click on the host name or planet letter to view its overview page.

## November 17, 2017

_**Note to our users:** We've changed our link format in the news so you can easily access overview pages for both planet hosts and their planets. Clicking on the host name or the planet letter will take you to object's respective overview page._

This week we've added eight confirmed planets, including [Ross 128](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=ROSS+128&type=PLANET_HOST)[b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=ROSS_128+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET), a rocky planet discovered to be only 11 light years from Earth, making it the second-closest known exo-Earth after [Proxima Centauri](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=Proxima+Cen&type=PLANET_HOST)[b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=Proxima+Cen+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET). Read the discovery paper ([Bonfils et al. 2017](https://www.eso.org/public/archives/releases/sciencepapers/eso1736/eso1736a.pdf)) and the [press release](http://eso.org/public/news/eso1736/).

The other planets (and their hosts) are [K2-136](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=K2-136&type=PLANET_HOST): [b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=k2-136+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET), [c](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=k2-136+c&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET), &[d](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=k2-136+d&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET); [K2-137](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=K2-137&type=PLANET_HOST): [b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=k2-137+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET); [Kepler-1652](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=kepler-1652&type=PLANET_HOST): [b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=kepler-1652+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET); [Kepler-1653](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=kepler-1653&type=PLANET_HOST): [b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=kepler-1653+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET), and [NGTS-1](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=NGTS-1&type=PLANET_HOST)[b](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/DisplayOverview/nph-DisplayOverview?objname=NGTS-1+b&type=CONFIRMED_PLANET), a hot Jupiter from the new [Next-Generation Transit Survey](http://www.ngtransits.org/) (NGTS). ## July 20, 2017

The Exoplanet Archive has integrated Jason Eastman's EXOFAST code into its suite of web services, which provides the tool with a more robust and stable home with several enhancements.

EXOFAST has been an important fitting tool for astronomers who want to use transit light curves or radial velocity data and various inputs to create models of planet systems. For more details, refer to [Eastman et al. (2013)](http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013PASP..125...83E).

The Exoplanet Archive's version of EXOFAST offers the same IDL-based calculations as the original code, and also provides sufficient back-end computing resources to enable Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis. In addition, the new EXOFAST draws on the archive's database of stellar and planetary parameters, which are updated weekly based on the current literature.

Interface enhancements include:

*   Interactive tables to view, sort and filter your uploaded data before running EXOFAST.
*   A preview pane to review the first 100 rows of your uploaded time series data, providing an opportunity to do a quick quality check before running EXOFAST.
*   Full-color, interactive plots of input files, including color, line and point control.
*   A temporary history of your results from recent EXOFAST sessions, saving you the time and effort of re-running analyses.

To access [EXOFAST](https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/ExoFAST/nph-exofast), click the **EXOFAST: Transit and RV Fitting**button on the archive home page under **Tools and Services**, or mouse over **Tools**in the menu bar to select it from the drop-down menu.
